### Extant sampling Extant bird masses were taken from the bird ecology database AVONET (Tobias et al., 2022) and combined with bird diet data from EltonTraits 1.0 Wilman et al., 2014 following the diet cut-offs in Table 2. The mass dataset consists of 8758 birds: 169 folivores, 931 frugivores, 1122 generalists, 475 granivores, 5061 invertivores, 450 nectarivores, 207 piscivores, 35 scavengers, and 308 tetrapod hunters. No additional extant birds are sampled for MA or FEA beyond the dataset of Miller et al., 2023, meaning these datasets consist of 141 birds: 9 folivores, 17 frugivores, 17 generalists, 8 husking granivores, 8 swallowing granivores, 43 invertivores, 7 nectarivores, 15 piscivores, 8 scavengers, and 9 tetrapod hunters. Five additional taxa were added to the ungual traditional morphometric (TM) dataset of Miller et al., 2023 to increase the sample of anisodactyl non-raptorial perching birds. Target taxa were identified from the literature as birds with well-recorded perching behaviour and no record of grasping or manipulating prey with the pes. This list of target taxa was sent in a formal loan request to Serina Brady of Carnegie Museum of Natural History, who provided photographs of all available specimens fitting the criteria. In total, the extant TM dataset includes 66 birds: 9 ground birds, 23 non-raptorial perching birds, 4 shrikes, 18 raptors taking large prey, and 12 raptors taking small prey. Of the 408 extant bird samples included in the skull TM analysis of Clark et al., 2023, 61 were removed due to not meeting the definition of any diet category in Table 2 (they were ‘in between’ diets as defined here, often with 50% of the diet from two sources). Thus, the final skull morphometric dataset consisted of 347 birds across 298 species: 9 folivores, 40 frugivores, 53 generalists, 5 granivores, 175 invertivores, 26 nectarivores, 27 piscivores, 4 scavengers, and 8 tetrapod hunters. ### Analytical techniques #### Body mass The granivore diet category was not split into husking and swallowing granivores; past work (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023) did not find the two subcategories to meaningfully differ in body mass. Average masses of groups were compared via phylogenetic HSD (pairwise function of R package RRPP [Collyer and Adams, 2018] used to compare group means). Diagnostic cut-off values between groups were found with the R package OptimalCutpoints (López-Ratón, 2014) version 1.1-5 by optimising the Youden index, with bootstrap estimation of 95% confidence intervals using the R package boot (Davison and Hinkley, 1997) version 1.3-28. #### Pedal traditional morphometrics, mechanical advantage, and finite element analysis The extant MA and FEA data in this study is unchanged from Miller et al., 2023, and new data collected from fossil specimens followed the same procedures as Miller et al., 2023. New fossil MA data were measured from the reconstructions in Figure 2 in CorelDraw X8. FEA models based on the reconstructions in Figure 2 were created and solved within HyperWorks 2022 Student Edition (HyperMesh and Optistruct, Altair Engineering, Inc, USA). We make the assumption that toothed and beaked models are directly comparable given that both operate under constraints of preventing breakage and deformation to the jaw (Miller and Pittman, 2021). Presence of a rhamphotheca is known to reduce stress experienced during a bite (Lautenschlager et al., 2013), so the beaked models all include a modelled rhamphotheca (Miller et al., 2022) to account for this effect. Pedal TM data are measured from scale photographs where available, though the five new included taxa were photographed without scale. All digits from a single individual were measured from a single photograph, so their relative scale is preserved. Our TM data is based solely on angles and length ratios, so this lack of scale should not be an issue. Pedal ecological categories for TM follow Miller et al., 2023; of note, we define raptors taking large prey as those with records of regularly taking prey which cannot be completely encircled by the pes, and raptors taking small prey as those without such records. As pointed out in Fowler et al., 2009, this division commonly follows phylogenetic lines, but we observe exceptions such as B. virginianus taking large prey (Artuso, 2020) and Buteogallus anthracinus not taking large prey (Schnell, 2020) clustering with birds in the same pedal ecological group rather than their phylogenetic relatives. All analyses of the data (PCA, FDA, pFDA, ancestral state reconstruction, etc.) were performed in R version 4.1.2 (R Development Core Team, 2020), with scripts and raw data including measurements and FE models available from Mendeley Data (https://doi.org/10.17632/7xtpbv27zh.3). #### Skull traditional morphometrics Clark et al., 2023 recently used skull traditional morphometrics to great effect in both differentiating extant bird diets and diagnosing the diet of longipterygid enantiornithines. Thus, we incorporate their data and methodology here as well to expand the evidence supporting our diet diagnoses. Measurements of skull and rostrum length for extant birds are unchanged from Clark et al., 2023. Clark et al., 2023 do not diagram their measurement landmarks, and the caudal landmark of the rostral length as ‘the caudal margin of the lacrimal (i.e. the rostral margin of the orbit)’ does not specify a dorsoventral height. So, for all new rostrum length measurements of bohaiornithids, we measured to the dorsoventral midpoint of the caudal margin of the ventral ramus of the lacrimal. Diet assignments of extant taxa were changed from those used by Clark et al., 2023 to those in Table 2 for consistency, following information in EltonTraits 1.0 (Wilman et al., 2014). We also use mass estimates for taxa from AVONET (Tobias et al., 2022), rather than those listed by Clark et al., 2023, for consistency within this work. Clark et al., 2023 visualise (their Figure 4) and generally interpret their skull morphometrics in terms of proportional rostral length (i.e. rostrum length divided by skull length) vs. log10 skull length. We have modified both of these factors in Figure 8. Firstly, we log10-transform both rostrum and skull length before taking their ratio, as this better normalises the distribution of proportional rostral length. Actual distribution of the data along this axis is minimally affected. Secondly, we use a relative skull length instead of absolute skull length. Absolute skull length is essentially a size proxy; Figure 8—figure supplement 1 shows skull length and body mass creating similar distributions, with the position of diet groups maintained relative to one another (while spreading more evenly along the x-axis when using body mass). This work already discusses body size as a diet proxy at length, so including it in morphometric discussion would be redundant. Through log10-log10 regression, we found that skull length generally increases with body mass with a scaling exponent of 2.75 (slightly negative allometry, R2 = 0.63) for the extant birds sampled. Thus we calculated relative skull length as: $$ relativeskulllength=\frac{(log_{10}(skulllength))^{2.7482}}{log_{10}(bodymass)} $$ Relative skull length approximates how much longer or shorter a given bird’s skull is than the expected length for a bird of the same body mass. #### Ancestral state reconstruction The backbone for the enantiornithine tree topology used in ancestral state reconstruction follows Wang et al., 2021b. This tree contains 34 of the 56 species used in ancestral state reconstruction. Additional taxa were grafted onto this backbone following Wang et al., 2022b; Liu et al., 2022; Wang, 2022a; O’Connor, 2009; Li et al., 2022; O’Connor et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2012a; Kurochkin et al., 2013; and Atterholt et al., 2018. Some taxa have only been included in one phylogenetic analysis, which placed said taxa within Bohaiornithidae, Longipterygidae, or Pengornithidae (e.g. Noguerornis placed within Longipterygidae by O’Connor, 2009). These taxa all lack the synapomorphies used to formally define the relevant clade, and their placements within them are likely artefacts of sharing a few characters while most data are missing. We therefore maintained monophyly of Bohaiornithidae, Longipterygidae, and Pengornithidae by placing these ambiguous taxa as sister to the family they were placed within. Time-scaling was performed using the R package paleotree (Bapst, 2012). All enantiornithine taxa were placed at their earliest occurrence, with species divergence arbitrarily chosen to take 1000 years. The enantiornithine phylogeny was rooted at 144 Ma after Cau, 2018 and Wang et al., 2021a. Ages of localities follow Zhong et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2006; Fregenal-Martínez, 2017; Lockley et al., 2018; Porfiri et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Napoli et al., 2021; Galobart et al., 2022; Montano et al., 2022; and Ramezani et al., 2022, with precise notes in the data repository (https://doi.org/10.17632/7xtpbv27zh.3). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa1)

Understanding the ecology including the dietary ecology of enantiornithines is challenging by all means. This work explores the possible trophic diversity of the "opposite-bird" enantiornithines by referring to the body mass, jaw mechanical advantage, finite element analysis of the jaw bones, and morphometrics of the claws and skull of both fossil and extant avian species. By incorporation the dietary information of longipterygids and pengornithinds, the authors predicted a wide variety of foods for enantiornithine ancestors. This indicates the evolutionary successes of enantiornitine during Cretaceous is very likely to have been driven by the wide range of recipes. I believe this work represented the most comprehensive analysis of enantiornithines' diet and trophic diversity by far and the first systematic dietary analysis of bohaiornithids, though the analysis themselves are largely based on the indirect evidence including jaw bone morphologies and claw and skull morphometrics. Anyway, I believe the authors did most the paleontologists could do, and I do not know whether the conclusions could be further supported by incorporating some geochemical data, as most of the specimens the authors analyzed were recovered from a small geographic area. The results also indicate that the developmental trajectories of enantiornithines, at least for jaw bones, might also have been diverse to some extent in response to the diverse ecological niches they adapted. My only concern regarding the analysis is to what extent the conclusions are convincing by comparing specimens representing various ontogenetic stages. This concern has been addressed in the revised manuscript. I believe the authors have almost exhausted all available methods, and I congratulate the authors for the detailed study they conducted.

Miller et al. take a variety of measurements and analytical techniques to assess the ecology of various species of the enantiornithine clade Bohaiornithidae. From this they suggest that the ancestral enantiornithine was a generalist and that the descendant clades occupied a breadth of niches similar to that of the radiation of derived birds after the K-Pg extinction.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa3)

Summary:

The authors use several quantitative approaches to characterize the feeding ecologies of bohaiornithid enantiornithines, including allometric data, mechanical advantage and finite element analyses of the jaw, and morphometric analyses of the claws. The authors combine their results with data for other enantiornithines collected from the literature to shed new insight on the ecological evolution of Enantiornithes as a clade.

Although the authors have taken steps to improve their paper, I generally find improvements unsatisfying, especially regarding my comments.

My remaining concerns:

Teeth: My concern here is not whether having teeth limits available niche space compared to having a keratinous beak. Rather, my concern regards how exploitation of the same niche space might be differently reflected in parameter space between birds with teeth and birds with beaks. Can we reliably expect two species that both eat seeds to occupy the same parameter space if, for example, distribution of stress/strain is across a series of teeth vs. across a more uniform beak? In this manuscript, the authors are clearly making this assumption, but that assumption is not made explicit, let alone justified. The authors should discuss this.

Cranial kinesis: As with teeth, my concern here regards our ability to compare data between birds with and without a flexible beak to mitigate forces when foraging. I appreciate that the functional complexity of the kinetic neognath skull precludes our ability to account for it in analyses such as these, but when comparisons are made using these analyses *specifically among neognaths*, we can reliably assume that we are comparing like to like - that is, we can assume that both have kinetic skulls, and so kinesis is reflected similarly in the data for each bird. Similarly, even if a comparison between two neognaths focuses exclusively on the mandible - in which cranial kinesis is not directly reflected - we can assume that those mandibles serve as comparisons between functionally similar systems. However, we cannot necessarily make those same assumptions when comparing the kinetic skull of a neognath to the akinetic skull of an enantiornithine. Indeed, even when focusing just on the mandible, can we reliably assume that data collected from an akinetic enantiornithine reflect the same comparative context as data collected from kinetic neognaths? I appreciate that the authors added a call for better functional understanding of bird cranial kinesis - a call I enthusiastically endorse - but the authors should still discuss how that current lack of understanding impacts interpretations of the comparisons they draw.

Finally, I still find the discussion to be overly long and lacking clear focus and organization. I again urge the authors to minimally consider adding subheadings to better allow the reader to follow the flow of ideas, and I second Reviewer #1's suggestion to add a "Conclusions" section.

claims.claim: Consumulite preservation is most likely with long gut retention times.

claims.claim: Preservation of plant propagules in the hindgut region implies prolonged retention where plant matter could ferment and break down.

claims.source: As with most bohaiornithids, the only diets which can be considered unlikely based on its mass are invertivory, granivory, and nectarivory.

claims.claim: Further ecological information for Beiguornis will require new techniques or more complete specimens.
claims.source: Further ecological information will require new techniques or more complete specimens.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current data for Beiguornis.

claims.claim: The results support hypotheses of raptorial behaviour in bohaiornithids, though not for every taxon.
claims.source: Our results support hypotheses of raptorial behaviour (Miller and Pittman, 2021; Wang, 2014a; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Li et al., 2014) in bohaiornithids, though not for every taxon.
claims.evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results showing some taxa with raptorial claw morphology.

claims.claim: Longusunguis is interpreted as a small predator adapted to take prey too large to be completely encircled by the pes.
claims.source: We interpret Longusunguis as a small predator adapted to take prey too large to be completely encircled by the pes, and Zhouornis as potentially a large predator whose talons were adapted to take prey which could be fully encircled by the pes.
claims.evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claims.claim: Zhouornis is interpreted as potentially a large predator whose talons were adapted to take prey which could be fully encircled by the pes.
claims.source: We interpret Longusunguis as a small predator adapted to take prey too large to be completely encircled by the pes, and Zhouornis as potentially a large predator whose talons were adapted to take prey which could be fully encircled by the pes.
claims.evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claims.claim: Sulcavis has a greatly enlarged and recurved digit I but lacks any enlarged opposed digit that could be used to grip.
claims.source: Sulcavis has a greatly enlarged and recurved digit I as expected in a raptor, but lacks any enlarged opposed digit that could be used to grip.
claims.evidence: This is based on the pedal TM data and description of Sulcavis morphology.

claims.claim: The unusual claw morphology of Sulcavis could be taphonomy obscuring the full extent of digit II or a different, unaccounted for use of the pes.
claims.source: As noted above, this could be taphonomy obscuring the full extent of digit II or a different, unaccounted for use of the pes.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for Sulcavis' unusual claw morphology.

claims.claim: The talons of Parabohaiornis are most akin to non-raptorial perching birds.
claims.source: The talons of Parabohaiornis are most akin to non-raptorial perching birds, and while the talons of Bohaiornis are between those of raptors and non-raptors we interpret them as non-raptorial given the taxon's herbivorous skull adaptations.
claims.evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claims.claim: The talons of Bohaiornis are interpreted as non-raptorial given the taxon's herbivorous skull adaptations.
claims.source: The talons of Parabohaiornis are most akin to non-raptorial perching birds, and while the talons of Bohaiornis are between those of raptors and non-raptors we interpret them as non-raptorial given the taxon's herbivorous skull adaptations.
claims.evidence: This is based on synthesis of pedal TM and jaw functional morphology data.

claims.claim: The alleged rangle in Bohaiornis has been reinterpreted as postmortem mineral growth.
claims.source: Note that the alleged rangle (raptorial gastroliths) used as previous evidence of raptorial behaviour in Bohaiornis (Li et al., 2014) has been reinterpreted as postmortem mineral growth (Liu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Specimens of Shenqiornis preserving talons are needed to opine on whether it was adapted for raptorial behaviour.
claims.source: Specimens of Shenqiornis preserving talons are needed to opine on whether it was adapted for raptorial behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current fossil material.

claims.claim: The study supports hypotheses of durophagy in bohaiornithids, though with the caveat that their adaptations are less extreme than what one usually considers an avian durophage.
claims.source: We also support hypotheses of durophagy (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; O'Connor et al., 2013; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Zhou et al., 2021) in bohaiornithids, though with the caveat that their adaptations are less extreme than what one usually considers an avian durophage.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of bohaiornithid jaw mechanics and strength to extant durophagous birds.

claims.claim: The first proposal of durophagy in a bohaiornithid was made in contrast to proposing most other enantiornithines as general insectivores limited to small arthropods with softer cuticles.
claims.source: The first proposal of durophagy in a bohaiornithid is made in contrast to proposing most other enantiornithines as 'general insectivore[s], limited to small arthropods with softer cuticles' (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids are durophagous in the sense that they have higher jaw strengths than other modelled enantiornithines.
claims.source: We support Bohaiornithids as durophagous in the sense that they have higher jaw strengths than other modelled enantiornithines (see above).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA results between bohaiornithids and other enantiornithine families.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids appear adapted for taking foods harder and tougher than soft-bodied arthropods.
claims.source: They appear adapted for taking foods harder and tougher than soft-bodied arthropods, but the same could be said for pengornithids.
claims.evidence: This is based on the FEA and mechanical advantage results.

claims.claim: In living birds, 'durophagy' typically refers to cracking hard foods like seeds or nuts within the beak.
claims.source: In living birds, 'durophagy' typically refers to cracking hard foods like seeds or nuts within the beak (Soons et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Soons et al., 2010 defining durophagy in birds.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw.
claims.source: As examined in the MA and FEA discussion sections, bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw; however, they lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores and fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage and FEA results comparing bohaiornithids to extant durophagous birds.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores.
claims.source: As examined in the MA and FEA discussion sections, bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw; however, they lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores and fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage results showing lower MA values in bohaiornithids than in husking granivores.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
claims.source: As examined in the MA and FEA discussion sections, bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw; however, they lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores and fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of mechanical advantage and FEA results between bohaiornithids and parrots.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant birds commonly considered durophages.
claims.source: Bohaiornithids, therefore, do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant birds commonly considered durophages.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison to extant durophagous birds.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithid tooth shape tightly clusters in phylomorphospace analyses.
claims.source: Bohaiornithid tooth shape does tightly cluster in the study's phylomorphospaces (Figures 4–6 in Zhou et al., 2021), but they notably tend to take a central position in the morphospace and overlap with purported granivores, insectivores, and piscivores.
claims.evidence: This is based on examination of figures in Zhou et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids tend to take a central position in tooth shape morphospace and overlap with purported granivores, insectivores, and piscivores.
claims.source: Bohaiornithid tooth shape does tightly cluster in the study's phylomorphospaces (Figures 4–6 in Zhou et al., 2021), but they notably tend to take a central position in the morphospace and overlap with purported granivores, insectivores, and piscivores.
claims.evidence: This is based on examination of figures in Zhou et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The similarity in bohaiornithid tooth shape is suggested to be driven by phylogeny rather than diet.
claims.source: Given this overlap and the ecological diversity within the group we support here, we suggest the similarity in bohaiornithid tooth shape is driven by phylogeny rather than, as proposed by Zhou et al., 2021, diet.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the dietary diversity found in this study contrasted with the morphological similarity in tooth shape.

claims.claim: The robust teeth in Bohaiornithidae may serve as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods effectively rather than adaptations to a specialised diet shared across the clade.
claims.source: The robust teeth in Bohaiornithidae may serve as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods effectively rather than adaptations to a specialised diet shared across the clade.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of bohaiornithid tooth morphology based on the dietary diversity found in the study.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids cover a greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families.
claims.source: Our data suggest that bohaiornithids cover a greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the dietary diversity found in bohaiornithids to that in longipterygids and pengornithids.

claims.claim: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment.
claims.source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left; though our mass results here suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected, contra Miller et al., 2022, see Body Mass Discussion), and pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The mass results in this study suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected.
claims.source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left; though our mass results here suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected, contra Miller et al., 2022, see Body Mass Discussion), and pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
claims.evidence: This is based on the refined body mass data and cut-offs presented in this study.

claims.claim: Pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet.
claims.source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left; though our mass results here suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected, contra Miller et al., 2022, see Body Mass Discussion), and pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show adaptations reminiscent of extant herbivores.
claims.source: In contrast, Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show adaptations reminiscent of extant herbivores while Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis were adapted for taking vertebrate prey.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage, FEA, and body mass results.

claims.claim: Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis were adapted for taking vertebrate prey.
claims.source: In contrast, Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show adaptations reminiscent of extant herbivores while Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis were adapted for taking vertebrate prey.
claims.evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results and other lines of evidence.

claims.claim: The differences in the mass and talon shape of Longusunguis and Zhouornis imply partitioning of the carnivorous niche.
claims.source: The differences in the mass and talon shape of the latter pair further imply partitioning of the carnivorous niche.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in body size and claw morphology between these two taxa.

claims.claim: The increased dietary breadth in Bohaiornithidae appears to stem from increased strength in the bohaiornithid skull.
claims.source: The increased dietary breadth in Bohaiornithidae appears to stem from increased strength in the bohaiornithid skull.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA results between bohaiornithids and other enantiornithine families.

claims.claim: Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae.
claims.source: In particular, Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae, which is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines (Wang et al., 2021b), and from the ancestral enantiornithine skull (Table 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of jaw strength and ancestral state reconstructions.

claims.claim: Pengornithid skull architecture is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines.
claims.source: In particular, Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae, which is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines (Wang et al., 2021b), and from the ancestral enantiornithine skull (Table 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021b.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithid skulls and teeth have been qualitatively described as robust in past works.
claims.source: Past works (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe et al., 2019) have qualitatively described bohaiornithid skulls and teeth as robust, though when using ACH to quantify robusticity bohaiornithids are not particularly remarkable.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang, 2014a and Chiappe et al., 2019.

claims.claim: When using ACH to quantify robusticity, bohaiornithids are not particularly remarkable.
claims.source: Past works (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe et al., 2019) have qualitatively described bohaiornithid skulls and teeth as robust, though when using ACH to quantify robusticity bohaiornithids are not particularly remarkable.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of ACH values between bohaiornithids and other enantiornithines.

claims.claim: There is a large difference in ACH between longipterygids and pengornithids.
claims.source: While there is a large difference between longipterygids (ACH 0.09–0.11, x̄ = 0.10; Miller et al., 2022) and pengornithids (ACH 0.22–0.23, x̄ = 0.23; Miller et al., 2023), bohaiornithid skulls (ACH 0.21–0.26, x̄ = 0.24) are only slightly more robust than those of pengornithids.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of ACH values from this study and previous studies.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithid skulls are only slightly more robust than those of pengornithids based on ACH.
claims.source: While there is a large difference between longipterygids (ACH 0.09–0.11, x̄ = 0.10; Miller et al., 2022) and pengornithids (ACH 0.22–0.23, x̄ = 0.23; Miller et al., 2023), bohaiornithid skulls (ACH 0.21–0.26, x̄ = 0.24) are only slightly more robust than those of pengornithids.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of ACH values.

claims.claim: Ancestral state reconstruction predicts Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae converged upon their level of robusticity from an ancestor whose ACH was between them and Longipterygidae.
claims.source: Ancestral state reconstruction (Figure 9—figure supplement 3K) predicts Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae converged upon this level of robusticity from an ancestor whose ACH was between them and Longipterygidae.
claims.evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: There is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families.
claims.source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA MWAM strain values between the three families.

claims.claim: Longipterygids have the weakest jaws among Jehol enantiornithine families.
claims.source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
claims.evidence: This is based on FEA results from Miller et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Pengornithid jaws are stronger than longipterygid jaws.
claims.source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
claims.evidence: This is based on FEA results from Miller et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithid jaws are stronger than pengornithid jaws.
claims.source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
claims.evidence: This is based on FEA results from this study.

claims.claim: Ancestral state reconstruction supports bohaiornithids and longipterygids diversifying from a common ancestor with pengornithid-like jaw strength.
claims.source: Ancestral state reconstruction supports bohaiornithids and longipterygids diversifying from a common ancestor with pengornithid-like jaw strength (Figure 9—figure supplement 3), though a lack of jaw strength data from families outside these three limits the reliability of this reconstruction.
claims.evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results, with acknowledgment of limitations.

claims.claim: An increase in jaw strength may have allowed Bohaiornithidae to process a wider variety of difficult-to-process foods than contemporary groups and ecologically diversify.
claims.source: An increase in jaw strength may have allowed Bohaiornithidae to process a wider variety of difficult-to-process foods than contemporary groups and ecologically diversify, but the poor resolution of relationships within and near the clade (Wang et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022; Table 1) makes this possibility difficult to test.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary significance of increased jaw strength, with acknowledgment of phylogenetic uncertainty.

claims.claim: The skull of Fortunguavis appears to have a robust surangular and pterygoid.
claims.source: For instance, the skull of Fortunguavis, while overall poorly preserved, does appear to have a robust surangular and pterygoid (Wang et al., 2014b) and is commonly recovered as sister to Bohaiornithidae.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014b.

claims.claim: Fortunguavis is commonly recovered as sister to Bohaiornithidae.
claims.source: For instance, the skull of Fortunguavis, while overall poorly preserved, does appear to have a robust surangular and pterygoid (Wang et al., 2014b) and is commonly recovered as sister to Bohaiornithidae.
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic summary in Table 1.

claims.claim: Strengthening of the skull may be present in more 'bohaiornithid-like' enantiornithines and even convergent between them.
claims.source: Strengthening of the skull may therefore be present in more 'bohaiornithid-like' enantiornithines (sensu Wang et al., 2022b) and even convergent between them.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the robust skull elements in Fortunguavis and phylogenetic relationships.

claims.claim: Shenqiornis is the geologically oldest bohaiornithid.
claims.source: Shenqiornis, the geologically oldest bohaiornithid, has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids (Figure 5) which does imply the skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
claims.evidence: This is based on the dating of the Qiaotou Formation described in the Methods.

claims.claim: Shenqiornis has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids.
claims.source: Shenqiornis, the geologically oldest bohaiornithid, has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids (Figure 5) which does imply the skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
claims.evidence: This is based on the FEA results in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
claims.source: Shenqiornis, the geologically oldest bohaiornithid, has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids (Figure 5) which does imply the skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the age of Shenqiornis and its jaw strength.

claims.claim: Longipterygids were limited by their weak and gracile jaws to relatively soft and compliant food sources.
claims.source: Longipterygids, conversely, were limited by their weak and gracile jaws to relatively soft and compliant food sources (Miller et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Whether the gracile jaws of longipterygids were adaptations to specialise in soft and compliant prey, or had unrelated benefits and coincidentally constrained their diet, remains unclear.
claims.source: However, whether the gracile jaws of longipterygids were adaptations to specialise in soft and compliant prey, or had unrelated benefits and coincidentally constrained their diet, remains unclear.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the evolutionary drivers of longipterygid jaw morphology.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithids and Pengornithids are notably larger than other Jehol enantiornithines.
claims.source: Bohaiornithids and Pengornithids are notably larger than other Jehol enantiornithines (Miller and Pittman, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller and Pittman, 2021.

claims.claim: Only Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis are interpreted as inhabiting similar niches to pengornithids among bohaiornithids.
claims.source: While we interpret only Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis as inhabiting similar niches to pengornithids, this size increase does make invertivory unlikely in every pengornithid and bohaiornithid.
claims.evidence: This is based on the dietary reconstructions from this study.

claims.claim: The size increase in bohaiornithids and pengornithids makes invertivory unlikely in every pengornithid and bohaiornithid.
claims.source: While we interpret only Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis as inhabiting similar niches to pengornithids, this size increase does make invertivory unlikely in every pengornithid and bohaiornithid.
claims.evidence: This is based on the body mass results and mass-diet relationships.

claims.claim: The food web of the Jehol Biota is generally understood to be dominated by small animals.
claims.source: The food web of the Jehol Biota is generally understood to be dominated by small animals (Matsukawa et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2019b), particularly in the Jiufotang formation in which bohaiornithids and pengornithids are most diverse.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsukawa et al., 2014 and O'Connor et al., 2019b.

claims.claim: Interspecific competition for invertebrates would be expected to be high in the Jehol ecosystem.
claims.source: Accordingly, one would expect interspecific competition for invertebrates to be high in this ecosystem.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the dominance of small animals in the Jehol food web.

claims.claim: Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae may be lineages which attempted to alleviate invertivorous competition by diversifying into consuming vertebrate or plant prey.
claims.source: Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae (alongside the ornithurine family Songlingornithidae; Miller and Pittman, 2021), then, may be lineages which attempted to alleviate invertivorous competition by diversifying into consuming vertebrate or plant prey.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary drivers of dietary diversification in these families.

claims.claim: Size increase in bohaiornithids and pengornithids is also commonly interpreted as defence against predation.
claims.source: Alternatively, size increase is also commonly interpreted as defence against predation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of a common interpretation in evolutionary biology.

claims.claim: Microraptor was definitely capable of preying on smaller enantiornithines.
claims.source: Microraptor was definitely capable of preying on smaller enantiornithines (O'Connor et al., 2011b) and the Jehol Biota had many carnivores larger than Microraptor (Matsukawa et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor et al., 2011b documenting predation on enantiornithines.

claims.claim: The Jehol Biota had many carnivores larger than Microraptor.
claims.source: Microraptor was definitely capable of preying on smaller enantiornithines (O'Connor et al., 2011b) and the Jehol Biota had many carnivores larger than Microraptor (Matsukawa et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsukawa et al., 2014 and O'Connor et al., 2019b.

claims.claim: The more abundant large carnivores in the Yixian formation may have provided pressure to grow larger when bohaiornithids and pengornithids first emerged.
claims.source: These possibilities need not be mutually exclusive: the more abundant large carnivores in the Yixian formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have provided pressure to grow larger when these clades first emerged, and the subsequent reduction in large carnivores by the Jiufotang formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have allowed them to further diversify.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary drivers of body size increase, supported by citation to Matsukawa et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The subsequent reduction in large carnivores by the Jiufotang formation may have allowed bohaiornithids and pengornithids to further diversify.
claims.source: These possibilities need not be mutually exclusive: the more abundant large carnivores in the Yixian formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have provided pressure to grow larger when these clades first emerged, and the subsequent reduction in large carnivores by the Jiufotang formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have allowed them to further diversify.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary drivers of dietary diversification, supported by citation to Matsukawa et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Ancestral state reconstruction predicts a concurrent increase in body mass for Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae near 125 Ma.
claims.source: Indeed, ancestral state reconstruction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) predicts a concurrent increase in body mass for Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae near 125 Ma.
claims.evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: Ancestral state reconstruction recovers the large mass of pengornithids as convergent, not present ancestrally in the clade.
claims.source: Interestingly, though, it recovers the large mass of pengornithids as convergent, not present ancestrally in the clade.
claims.evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: The convergent large mass in pengornithids is driven by the earliest pengornithid, Eopengornis, being smaller than its more recent relatives.
claims.source: This is driven by the earliest pengornithid, Eopengornis, being smaller than its more recent relatives.
claims.evidence: This is based on body mass estimates for Eopengornis compared to other pengornithids.

claims.claim: No bohaiornithid is known from the same time frame as Eopengornis.
claims.source: No bohaiornithid is known from this time frame, so we cannot yet comment on if their increased body mass is similarly convergent or ancestral to Bohaiornithidae as a whole.
claims.evidence: This is based on the fossil record and dating of bohaiornithid specimens.

claims.claim: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes likely had a body mass near 200 g.
claims.source: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes likely had a body mass near 200 g (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Table 7), pointing to frugivory or generalist feeding.
claims.evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction of body mass.

claims.claim: The body mass of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes points to frugivory or generalist feeding.
claims.source: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes likely had a body mass near 200 g (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Table 7), pointing to frugivory or generalist feeding.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mass-diet relationships established in this study.

results.result: Bohaiornithidae exhibits greater ecological diversity than other enantiornithine families, with different genera occupying distinct dietary niches: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis resemble plant-eating birds, Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores, Zhouornis resembles frugivores/generalists, and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis show mixed affinities.
results.evaluation: This major finding is supported by convergent evidence from multiple independent analyses (body mass C22, mechanical advantage C33-C34, FEA C35-C38, and pedal morphometrics C39-C41). The dietary assignments for each genus are based on quantitative comparisons to extant birds across these multiple lines of evidence, providing robust support for the ecological diversity claim.

results.result: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis could have sustained herbivory through oral processing and/or hindgut fermentation despite likely lacking crops and gizzards, based on analogies to herbivorous lizards and birds with hindgut specialization.
results.evaluation: While the jaw morphology data (C68) supports herbivorous adaptations, the mechanism for plant processing remains speculative. The analogies to lizards (C54-C55) and hindgut fermentation in birds (C58-C62) are plausible but indirect. The alternative 'fallback food' hypothesis (C70-C73) is equally viable, and direct evidence of digestive specialization is absent.

results.result: Zhouornis is interpreted as either frugivorous or generalist based on its strong jaw, large body size, and intermediate claw morphology, with potential for limited macrocarnivory similar to the barred owl.
results.evaluation: The dietary interpretation is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: FEA showing the strongest bohaiornithid jaw (C74), body mass data (C77), mechanical advantage predictions (C79), and pedal morphometrics (C80). The barred owl analogy (C86-C88) provides a reasonable modern comparison for the predicted ecological role.

results.result: Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis have ambiguous dietary diagnoses with piscivory, generalist feeding, and folivory all plausible, requiring additional lines of evidence for resolution.
results.evaluation: The authors explicitly acknowledge the uncertainty (C89, C109) due to intermediate FEA values (C92), poor mechanical advantage discrimination (C95), and conflicting signals from different analyses. For Longusunguis, pedal morphology (C98) and tooth shape (C99-C100) favor carnivory over skull morphometrics (C101), but the overall picture remains unclear.

results.result: Raptorial behavior is supported in some but not all bohaiornithids: Longusunguis adapted for large prey, Zhouornis potentially for small prey, while Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show non-raptorial adaptations.
results.evaluation: The pedal morphometric data (C40-C41) provides quantitative support for differentiating raptorial from non-raptorial taxa. The interpretations for Longusunguis (C114) and the non-raptorial nature of Bohaiornis/Parabohaiornis (C118-C119) are well-supported by claw shape analysis. The unusual morphology of Sulcavis (C116-C117) is appropriately treated as uncertain.

results.result: Bohaiornithids show adaptations for durophagy relative to other enantiornithines but lack the extreme specializations of extant avian durophages like parrots and husking granivores.
results.evaluation: The comparative FEA and mechanical advantage data clearly demonstrate that bohaiornithids have stronger jaws than other enantiornithines (C124) and resemble husking granivores in some metrics (C127), but fall short of parrots in force production (C128-C129). This nuanced conclusion appropriately qualifies the durophagy hypothesis.

results.result: Bohaiornithids show greater ecological breadth than longipterygids and pengornithids, potentially stemming from increased jaw strength that represents an evolutionary trajectory distinct from the weaker longipterygid jaws.
results.evaluation: The stepwise increase in jaw strength across families (C150-C153) is quantitatively demonstrated through FEA data. The correlation between jaw strength and dietary diversity (C142) is supported by the comparative data from all three families. The ancestral state reconstruction (C154) provides evolutionary context, though the authors appropriately note limitations.

results.result: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes is reconstructed as an arboreal generalist feeder with body mass near 200g, intermediate mechanical advantage, and claw shape dissimilar to extant birds, though this reconstruction is limited by sparse sampling of early-diverging taxa.
results.evaluation: While the ancestral state reconstruction follows appropriate methods and integrates multiple data types (C179-C188), the authors explicitly acknowledge critical limitations: many early-diverging taxa have unknown diets (C193), the reconstruction may be biased toward pengornithids due to sampling (C194), and further study is needed (C195). The uncertainty is appropriately recognized.

results.result: Enantiornithines achieved substantial ecological diversification within 25 million years of Ornithothoraces origin, suggesting that crown bird traits like edentulism and cranial kinesis cannot fully explain crown bird ecological success, and that Ornithothoraces-level traits may be more important.
results.evaluation: The temporal calculation (C197) is straightforward given the cited dates. The comparison to Neoaves diversification (C198) provides appropriate context. The inference that crown bird traits are insufficient (C199) logically follows from the demonstrated rapid enantiornithine diversification without these traits. The recommendation to study Ornithothoraces-level traits (C202) is a reasonable conclusion.

results.result: Body mass analysis was expanded to 8,758 bird species using the AVONET database, improving resolution of mass-diet relationships and establishing quantitative cut-offs between diet categories.
results.evaluation: The expanded dataset (C51) represents a substantial improvement over previous studies. The statistical approach using phylogenetic HSD and Youden index optimization is appropriate. The resulting cut-offs provide quantitative thresholds for dietary inference, though the method assumes mass-diet relationships are consistent across phylogeny.

results.result: The study employs mechanical advantage and finite element analysis as complementary approaches to assess jaw function, with MA examining force-speed trade-offs and FEA comparing relative jaw strength under standardized loading.
results.evaluation: The methodological framework is well-established in the literature (C33, C35, C38) and appropriately applied. The combination of MA and FEA provides complementary information about jaw function. However, the authors note that MA has limited discriminatory power for some diet categories, which is an appropriate acknowledgment of method limitations.

results.result: The study expands previous analytical frameworks by incorporating skull traditional morphometrics, using modified methodology from Clark et al. 2023 with alternate body mass sources and size correction.
results.evaluation: The methodological expansion (C42) is justified by successful application in longipterygids (C43). The modifications to the Clark et al. approach (C45) are reasonable attempts to improve the analysis. However, the authors later acknowledge uncertainty about whether skull morphometrics are appropriate for bohaiornithids due to potential developmental constraints.

results.result: The large body size of bohaiornithids and pengornithids may have evolved either to escape invertivorous competition or as defense against predation, with ancestral state reconstruction suggesting concurrent mass increase around 125 Ma.
results.evaluation: While the body size increase is well-documented (C164, C175) and the ecological context is established (C167, C171-C172), the evolutionary drivers remain speculative. Both the competition hypothesis (C169) and predation hypothesis (C170) are plausible but untestable with current data. The convergent evolution in pengornithids (C176-C177) adds complexity but doesn't resolve the causal mechanism.

results.result: Bohaiornithid tooth shape clusters tightly in morphospace but overlaps with multiple diet categories, suggesting tooth similarity is driven by phylogeny rather than diet, with teeth potentially serving as general-use tools.
results.evaluation: The observation of tight clustering with dietary overlap (C131-C132) combined with the dietary diversity found in this study provides strong support for the phylogenetic signal interpretation (C133). The general-use tool hypothesis (C134) is a reasonable inference, though it remains speculative without functional testing.

results.result: Quantitative analysis using average cranial height shows bohaiornithid skulls are only slightly more robust than pengornithids, with ancestral state reconstruction suggesting convergent evolution of this robusticity level.
results.evaluation: The ACH measurements provide quantitative support for the claim that bohaiornithids are not exceptionally robust (C146, C148), contradicting qualitative descriptions (C145). The large difference between longipterygids and the other two families (C147) is clear from the data. The ancestral state reconstruction (C149) appropriately uses quantitative methods.

results.result: Flight capabilities defining Ornithothoraces may drive rapid diversification by providing access to multiple vertical strata and larger home ranges, increasing resource availability.
results.evaluation: While the ecological advantages of flight are well-established (C204-C205), the causal link to diversification rate (C207) is speculative. This hypothesis is presented as a suggestion for future research rather than a tested conclusion, which is appropriate given the available data.

results.result: Bohaiornithids exhibit greater ecological diversity than other enantiornithine families, with different genera occupying distinct dietary niches: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis resemble plant-eating birds, Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores, Zhouornis is similar to frugivores/generalists, and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis show mixed dietary signals. This diversity stems from increased jaw strength in bohaiornithids.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states this work 'represented the most comprehensive analysis of enantiornithines' diet and trophic diversity by far and the first systematic dietary analysis of bohaiornithids.' The editor notes the study 'explores numerous lines of evidence for the surprisingly diverse diets' and calls it 'important.' Reviewer 2 finds the proposal 'curious, thought-provoking' and approves the manuscript. The comprehensive dataset and multiple analytical approaches are affirmed.

results.result: The ancestral enantiornithine is reconstructed as an arboreal generalist feeder with body mass near 200g, intermediate mechanical advantage, jaw strain of 227 µε, and claw shape dissimilar to extant birds. However, more quantitative data from across the enantiornithine tree is needed to refine this prediction, as the diet of many earliest-diverging taxa remains obscure.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the comprehensive methodology, Reviewer 1 notes 'the analysis themselves are largely based on the indirect evidence' and expresses concern about 'to what extent the conclusions are convincing by comparing specimens representing various ontogenetic stages.' The authors themselves acknowledge limitations, stating the ancestral diet 'remains somewhat speculative' and that their reconstruction 'in many ways resembles a smaller pengornithid' due to sampling bias. The need for more data is explicitly stated.

results.result: By the Early Cretaceous (~120 Ma), enantiornithines had diversified into a variety of ecological niches comparable to crown birds after the K-Pg extinction, achieving this diversity in only 25 million years. This suggests that traits unique to crown birds (edentulism, cranial kinesis) cannot completely explain their ecological success, and that Ornithothoraces-level traits may be more important.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises fundamental concerns about comparing toothed enantiornithines to beaked crown birds, stating 'my concern regards how exploitation of the same niche space might be differently reflected in parameter space between birds with teeth and birds with beaks' and noting 'the authors are clearly making this assumption, but that assumption is not made explicit, let alone justified.' Similarly, regarding cranial kinesis, the reviewer questions 'can we reliably assume that data collected from an akinetic enantiornithine reflect the same comparative context as data collected from kinetic neognaths?' These methodological concerns directly impact the validity of comparing diversification patterns.

results.result: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis could have sustained folivory through oral processing and/or hindgut fermentation despite likely lacking crops and gizzards. Their jaw adaptations indicate evolutionary pressure for consuming plant material, possibly as fallback foods during periods of climate instability in the Jehol ecosystem.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this interpretation. Reviewer 1 notes 'the developmental trajectories of enantiornithines, at least for jaw bones, might also have been diverse to some extent in response to the diverse ecological niches they adapted,' which aligns with this functional interpretation. The analogies to herbivorous lizards and birds with hindgut fermentation are not questioned.

results.result: Zhouornis has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids and is interpreted as either frugivorous or generalist, with body mass (758g) ruling out granivory/nectarivory. If generalist, it may have overlapped ecologically with Pengornis but differed in body size, potentially representing different approaches to exploiting prey resources.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the dietary reconstruction of Zhouornis. The integration of multiple lines of evidence (FEA, mechanical advantage, body mass, pedal morphology) is consistent with the comprehensive approach praised by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'did most the paleontologists could do' with available methods.

results.result: Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis have less clear dietary diagnoses, with evidence pointing to piscivory, generalist feeding, and possibly folivory. FEA provides limited discrimination, mechanical advantage has poor predictive power, and pedal morphology suggests carnivory for Longusunguis but is ambiguous for the others. Additional lines of evidence are necessary for confident diagnosis.
results.evaluation: The authors explicitly acknowledge uncertainty for these taxa, stating 'even with four lines of evidence the dietary diagnosis of these three taxa remains tentative.' Reviewer 1's concern about ontogenetic stages is particularly relevant here, as is the acknowledgment that Shenqiornis skull reconstruction relies on cf. Sulcavis material, 'artificially inflating the functional similarity of the two genera.' The call for additional methods (dental microwear, muscle reconstruction, stable isotopes) indicates recognized limitations.

results.result: Pedal morphology supports raptorial behavior in some bohaiornithids: Longusunguis is interpreted as adapted for large prey, Zhouornis for small prey, while Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show non-raptorial morphology. Sulcavis has unusual claw morphology that may reflect taphonomy or unaccounted-for function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the pedal morphometric interpretations. The reinterpretation of alleged 'rangle' in Bohaiornis as postmortem mineral growth (citing Liu et al., 2021) demonstrates appropriate critical evaluation of previous claims. The acknowledgment of uncertainty for Sulcavis and need for better Shenqiornis specimens shows appropriate caution.

results.result: Bohaiornithids are durophagous in having higher jaw strength than other enantiornithines and being adapted for harder foods than soft-bodied arthropods, but they lack the extreme adaptations of extant durophages like husking granivores or parrots. Their robust teeth may serve as general-use tools rather than specializations for a single diet, with similarity driven by phylogeny rather than diet.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this nuanced interpretation of durophagy. The distinction between relative strength within enantiornithines versus absolute comparison to extant specialized durophages is not questioned. This careful interpretation aligns with Reviewer 1's observation that the authors 'did most the paleontologists could do' with available evidence.

results.result: There is a stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families (longipterygids weakest, pengornithids intermediate, bohaiornithids strongest), with ancestral state reconstruction suggesting bohaiornithids and longipterygids diversified from a pengornithid-like ancestor. This increased strength may have enabled bohaiornithids to process diverse difficult foods and ecologically diversify, predating 124 Ma based on Shenqiornis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the FEA comparisons between families or the stepwise pattern. However, the authors acknowledge 'poor resolution of relationships within and near the clade' makes testing evolutionary hypotheses difficult, and 'lack of jaw strength data from families outside these three limits the reliability of this reconstruction.' The pattern is accepted but evolutionary interpretation remains tentative.

results.result: Body mass has a strong effect on bird diet, so estimating mass of extinct birds helps narrow dietary possibilities. The AVONET database allows expansion of the mass-diet dataset to 8758 of 9994 recognized bird species.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the body mass methodology or its utility for dietary inference. Reviewer 1 notes the 'large amount of data the authors collected forms a solid dataset.' The use of AVONET represents a methodological improvement expanding the comparative framework.

results.result: Mechanical advantage examines trade-offs between bite speed and force. Three versions of MA are collected alongside other functional indices. FEA models forces on irregular structures during biting, allowing comparison of relative jaw strength under constant relative load.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these methodological approaches. The editor notes 'the methods might in principle be extensible to other limbed vertebrates, although there are concerns regarding some of the details.' Reviewer 3's concerns focus on comparing toothed vs. toothless birds and kinetic vs. akinetic skulls, not on the validity of MA or FEA methods themselves.

results.result: Traditional morphometrics of pedal unguals can differentiate raptorial from non-raptorial birds and potentially specific raptorial behaviors. Skull TM, recently successful for longipterygids, is incorporated with modifications including alternate body mass/diet sources and size correction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the morphometric methodologies. Reviewer 1 notes this represents 'the most comprehensive analysis' and that the authors 'have almost exhausted all available methods.' The expansion beyond previous frameworks is viewed positively.

results.result: Bohaiornithids and pengornithids are notably larger than other Jehol enantiornithines, making invertivory unlikely. This size increase may reflect either alleviating invertivorous competition in the small-animal-dominated Jehol ecosystem or defense against predation. Ancestral state reconstruction suggests concurrent mass increase near 125 Ma, though pengornithid large size appears convergent.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these ecological interpretations of body size evolution. The hypotheses about competitive release and predator defense are presented as alternatives rather than definitive conclusions, which is appropriate given the evidence. The ancestral state reconstructions are accepted as part of the comprehensive analytical framework.

results.result: Ornithothoraces is defined by flight adaptations. Flight allows access to multiple vertical strata and larger home ranges, providing greater resource variety and potentially driving repeated rapid diversification in ornithothoracine lineages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this evolutionary interpretation. Reviewer 2 finds the comparison between enantiornithine and crown bird diversification 'curious, thought-provoking.' The hypothesis about flight capabilities enabling diversification is presented appropriately as a potential explanation rather than proven fact.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the major finding of dietary diversity in enantiornithines as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from multiple analyses (body mass, mechanical advantage, FEA, pedal morphometrics). Peer review affirms this as 'the most comprehensive analysis' with 'numerous lines of evidence.' Both recognize the robust multi-method approach, though peer review also includes claims about jaw strength evolution (C135-C142) not in OpenEval R1.

Perfect agreement on Zhouornis dietary interpretation as SUPPORTED. Both cite multiple lines of evidence (FEA, body mass, mechanical advantage, pedal morphology) supporting the vertebrate predator interpretation. OpenEval provides detailed barred owl analogy; peer review notes no challenges were raised and aligns with the comprehensive approach praised by reviewers.

Complete agreement on UNCERTAIN evaluation for Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis diets. Both cite conflicting signals from different analyses, intermediate FEA values, poor mechanical advantage discrimination, and explicitly acknowledge the tentative nature of conclusions. Peer review adds concern about ontogenetic stages and skull reconstruction reliability.

Both evaluate pedal morphometric interpretations as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative differentiation of raptorial vs. non-raptorial taxa and appropriate treatment of Sulcavis uncertainty. Peer review confirms no challenges were raised and notes the reinterpretation of alleged 'rangle' in Bohaiornis demonstrates critical evaluation.

Both evaluate body mass methodology as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the expanded dataset and appropriate statistical approach (phylogenetic HSD, Youden index). Peer review confirms the 'large amount of data' forms a 'solid dataset' and AVONET represents methodological improvement. No challenges to the approach.

Both evaluate mechanical advantage and FEA methods as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes well-established literature basis and complementary information from MA and FEA. Peer review accepts these methods, though editor notes concerns about 'some of the details' and Reviewer 3 questions comparing toothed vs. toothless birds (addressed in R9/R3 pairing).

Both evaluate skull morphometric methodology as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes justified expansion and reasonable modifications to Clark et al. approach, while acknowledging later uncertainty about appropriateness for bohaiornithids. Peer review views this as part of 'the most comprehensive analysis' with no direct challenges to the methods themselves.

Both evaluate body size evolution interpretations as UNCERTAIN (OpenEval) or SUPPORTED (peer review). OpenEval emphasizes that evolutionary drivers (competition vs. predation) remain speculative and untestable. Peer review accepts the ecological interpretations but notes hypotheses are presented as alternatives rather than definitive conclusions, suggesting alignment on tentative nature.

OpenEval rates flight-diversification link as UNCERTAIN, noting the causal connection is speculative and presented as future research suggestion. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, finding it 'curious, thought-provoking' and appropriately presented as potential explanation rather than proven fact. Difference reflects interpretation of how speculative hypotheses should be classified.

Both evaluate ancestral state reconstruction as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval emphasizes critical limitations: unknown diets for early taxa, sampling bias toward pengornithids, need for further study. Peer review adds concerns about indirect evidence and ontogenetic stage comparisons, noting the reconstruction 'remains somewhat speculative.' Strong agreement on uncertainty despite comprehensive methodology.

OpenEval evaluates rapid diversification claims as SUPPORTED based on temporal calculations and logical inference. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, raising fundamental methodological concerns about comparing toothed enantiornithines to beaked crown birds and akinetic to kinetic skulls.
